biometric_photos.name: Biometric photos (×6)
biometric_photos.notes: Order 6: visa form needs 2, more for residence permit + Anmeldung in Germany.

birth_certificate.name: Birth certificate
birth_certificate.where: Civil registry office at your place of birth
birth_certificate.notes: Get a multilingual/international extract if your country issues one — it can save translation cost.

police_clearance.name: Police clearance (Bulletin n°3)
police_clearance.where: Tribunal de 1ère Instance OR online: service-public.ma
police_clearance.notes: Must be issued within 3 months of visa appointment. Request 2 copies.

marriage_certificate.name: Marriage certificate
marriage_certificate.where: Bureau d'État Civil where marriage was registered
marriage_certificate.notes: Only needed if applying for family reunification later. Apostilled + translated.

children_birth_certs.name: Children's birth certificates
children_birth_certs.where: Bureau d'État Civil where each child was registered
children_birth_certs.notes: Apostille + sworn translation per child. Only if bringing children.

bac_diploma.name: Bac diploma
bac_diploma.where: Académie Régionale de l'Éducation et de la Formation (where you sat the Bac)
bac_diploma.notes: Original or certified copy. If you only have a duplicata, it must be apostilled too.

bac_transcripts.name: Bac transcripts (Relevés de notes)
bac_transcripts.notes: Both years of Bac required. Apostille each page.

higher_ed_diploma.name: Higher-education diploma
higher_ed_diploma.where: Your university's Bureau de la Scolarité
higher_ed_diploma.notes: Bachelor / Master / DUT / etc. Original + apostille + sworn translation.

higher_ed_transcripts.name: Higher-education transcripts
higher_ed_transcripts.notes: All years. Cumulative GPA helps for APS evaluation.

aps_certificate.name: APS certificate (Akademische Prüfstelle)
aps_certificate.where: The APS office for your country (German embassy / DAAD)
aps_certificate.notes: Required for some countries (e.g. China, India, Vietnam, Pakistan). Start it first — processing can take 6–20 weeks. Submit all academic records since high school.

anabin_check.name: Anabin recognition lookup
anabin_check.notes: Verify your university and degree are listed as H+ in the Anabin database. Take a screenshot for your records — no formal certificate needed.

studienkolleg.name: Studienkolleg admission (if your diploma does not directly qualify)
studienkolleg.where: Apply via your target German university
studienkolleg.notes: Whether you need it depends on how your secondary diploma compares to the German Abitur. Check anabin / your target university.

german_b1.name: German B1 certificate (Goethe / telc / ÖSD)
german_b1.where: A Goethe-Institut, telc or ÖSD test centre in your country
german_b1.notes: B1 is the minimum for an Ausbildung visa. Most employers prefer B2.

german_b2.name: German B2 certificate (Goethe / telc / ÖSD)
german_b2.where: A Goethe-Institut, telc or ÖSD test centre in your country
german_b2.notes: Required for most Studium programmes. Some require TestDaF or DSH-2 instead.

visa_application_form.name: National D-visa application form
visa_application_form.where: Download from the German mission's site (rk.diplo.de) or your visa centre
visa_application_form.notes: Fill 2 copies in German or English. Sign each page.

cv_german.name: CV in German (Lebenslauf)
cv_german.where: Self-prepared — use the CV builder on this site
cv_german.notes: Tabular format only. Photo top-right. Sign and date at the bottom.

motivation_letter.name: Motivation letter (Anschreiben) in German
motivation_letter.where: Self-prepared — use the Anschreiben generator on this site
motivation_letter.notes: One page max. Address it to the German consul or your future employer/university.

ausbildungsvertrag.name: Ausbildungsvertrag (signed Ausbildung contract)
ausbildungsvertrag.notes: Must include start date, salary, training duration, IHK/HWK registration number.

taetigkeitsbeschreibung.name: Tätigkeitsbeschreibung (job description)
taetigkeitsbeschreibung.notes: Required for the Bundesagentur Vorab check. Employer fills the standardized form.

vorab_zustimmung.name: Vorab-Zustimmung (pre-approval)
vorab_zustimmung.notes: Cuts visa processing from ~8 months to ~2 months. Worth pushing your employer to obtain.

university_admission.name: University admission letter (Zulassung)
university_admission.notes: Final Zulassung or Bedingungszulassung both accepted. Original + 2 copies.

sperrkonto.name: Sperrkonto (€11,904 blocked account)
sperrkonto.notes: Mandatory for Studium; Ausbildung trainees with salary < €934/mo also need it. ~€89 setup fee + the €11,904 deposit (paid back to you in monthly instalments after arrival).

verpflichtungserklaerung.name: Verpflichtungserklärung (sponsor declaration)
verpflichtungserklaerung.where: Sponsor in Germany goes to their local Ausländerbehörde
verpflichtungserklaerung.notes: Alternative to Sperrkonto. Sponsor must prove sufficient income. ~€29 fee paid by sponsor.

bank_statements.name: Bank statements (last 3 months)
bank_statements.notes: Sometimes requested as supporting evidence even when a Sperrkonto is in place.

travel_health_insurance.name: Travel health insurance (first 90 days)
travel_health_insurance.notes: Must cover ≥ €30,000 of medical costs and the entire pre-residence-permit period.

accommodation_proof.name: Accommodation proof (Wohnungsgeberbestätigung or hotel reservation)
accommodation_proof.where: Your future German landlord OR hotel booking site
accommodation_proof.notes: A signed Wohnungsgeberbestätigung is best. Hotel reservation for the first 4 weeks is acceptable while you find a long-term flat.

visa_fee.name: National D-visa fee (€75)
visa_fee.notes: Non-refundable. Payment method depends on the visa centre.

visa_appointment.name: Visa appointment
visa_appointment.where: The official German visa centre for your country (VFS Global, TLScontact, or the embassy/consulate)
visa_appointment.notes: Book early — slots are often 1–3 months out, longer in summer. Any service fee is separate from the visa fee.

german_a1_cert.name: German A1 certificate (Goethe / telc / ÖSD)
german_a1_cert.where: A Goethe-Institut, telc or ÖSD test centre in your country
german_a1_cert.notes: Mandatory for spousal family reunification (Ehegattennachzug) under §28 AufenthG. Exceptions: spouse holds a university degree from a German-speaking country, or applicant is over 67.

sponsor_permit_copy.name: Sponsor's residence permit (Aufenthaltstitel) — copy
sponsor_permit_copy.notes: A copy of their current Aufenthaltstitel. Ensure it covers the reunion period and allows family reunification.

sponsor_income_proof.name: Sponsor's income proof (last 3 salary slips + tax return)
sponsor_income_proof.where: Your sponsor's employer / tax office in Germany
sponsor_income_proof.notes: Must show sufficient income to support the family. Minimum threshold varies by Bundesland — check with the responsible Ausländerbehörde.

sponsor_housing_proof.name: Housing proof — Wohnflächennachweis (min. 12 m² per person)
sponsor_housing_proof.notes: Shows the accommodation meets minimum space requirements. A landlord confirmation (Wohnungsgeberbestätigung) or lease agreement is usually sufficient.

schengen_visa_form.name: Schengen C visa application form
schengen_visa_form.where: Download from the German mission's website or the visa centre (VFS / TLScontact)
schengen_visa_form.notes: Complete in German or English. Sign every page. Bring 2 identical copies to your appointment.

travel_insurance_tourist.name: Travel health insurance (min. €30,000 coverage)
travel_insurance_tourist.where: Online: Coracle, MAWISTA, DR-WALTER, Allianz Travel
travel_insurance_tourist.notes: Must cover the full Schengen trip duration plus entry/exit days. Minimum coverage €30,000. Must include repatriation costs.

flight_reservation.name: Round-trip flight reservation
flight_reservation.where: Your airline or online booking site
flight_reservation.notes: A reservation confirmation is enough — you do not need to buy the ticket before the visa is granted. Many services offer free 24-hour holds.

accommodation_tourist.name: Accommodation proof for the entire stay
accommodation_tourist.where: Hotel, hostel, Airbnb confirmation — or a host's signed invitation letter
accommodation_tourist.notes: Every night of the trip must be accounted for. If staying with a host in Germany, a signed Verpflichtungserklärung (invitation/guarantee letter) issued at the Ausländerbehörde is preferred.

financial_means_proof.name: Proof of sufficient funds (bank statements — last 3 months)
financial_means_proof.notes: Germany requires approx. €45–€100 per day of stay. Statements must show regular income or sufficient savings. Some missions also accept a sponsor guarantee.

employment_ties_proof.name: Proof of ties to home country (employment/enrolment letter or property deed)
employment_ties_proof.where: Your employer, university, or property registry
employment_ties_proof.notes: Demonstrates you will return after the trip. A leave-approval letter from your employer, a student enrolment certificate, or proof of property ownership are the most common forms.

schengen_visa_fee.name: Schengen C visa fee (€90)
schengen_visa_fee.where: Paid at your appointment (cash or card — check with the visa centre)
schengen_visa_fee.notes: Non-refundable even if the visa is refused. Some countries have reduced fees under bilateral agreements (e.g. Armenia, Azerbaijan: €35). Children under 6: free. Children 6–12: €45.

schengen_appointment.name: Visa appointment at the German mission or visa centre
schengen_appointment.where: The German embassy, consulate or authorised visa centre (VFS Global, TLScontact) for your country
schengen_appointment.notes: Book as early as possible — slots in peak season (June–August) can be 4–8 weeks out. Biometric fingerprints are captured at the appointment.

ausbildung.p1: Germany's Ausbildung (dual vocational training) system is one of the most sought-after immigration pathways for {country} nationals. The national D-visa for vocational training, governed by §17a of the German Residence Act (AufenthG), entitles you to complete a 2–3-year accredited training programme at a German company while earning a salary. Unlike Studium, Ausbildung requires no university degree — a secondary school diploma (Baccalauréat or equivalent) and a signed training contract are the core requirements.
ausbildung.p2: Document authentication is a decisive factor in how quickly applicants from {country} can submit their visa file. Germany requires authentication by {authMethod} for all official documents issued in {country}, including your birth certificate, diplomas, school transcripts, and police clearance. The {authMethod} step costs €{authFeeMin}–{authFeeMax} per document and adds {authDaysMin}–{authDaysMax} days to your preparation. Sworn German translations are also mandatory for all non-German documents — plan for an additional €20–60 per page from a certified translator.
ausbildung.p3: The visa process itself begins with a German B1 language certificate (Goethe, telc or ÖSD), since this is the minimum required for most Ausbildung visas. Your future employer in Germany files a Vorab-Zustimmung (preliminary approval) with the Bundesagentur für Arbeit — if granted, visa processing shrinks from around 8 months to roughly 2 months. Financial proof is also required: depending on your training salary, you may need a Sperrkonto (blocked account) holding €11,904 for the year, or an alternative guarantee (Verpflichtungserklärung) from a German-resident sponsor.
ausbildung.p4: From {country}, the realistic end-to-end timeline — from gathering documents to your first day at work in Germany — is {timelineMin}–{timelineMax} weeks. Visa appointment slots at the German mission or TLScontact/VFS centre in {country} tend to fill up months in advance. Submit your complete dossier at the appointment: incomplete files are not accepted and no refunds are given. The national D-visa fee is €{visaFee}, payable on the day.

studium.p1: Germany is one of the top destinations in the world for international students — and for {country} nationals, a German Studium (university study) visa opens the door to tuition-free or low-fee education at world-ranked institutions. The national D-visa for higher education is governed by §16b AufenthG and allows you to enrol in a full Bachelor's, Master's, or PhD programme.
studium.p2: All academic documents from {country} must be authenticated by {authMethod} before they can be submitted to the German mission. This applies to your Baccalauréat diploma, transcripts, higher-education diplomas, and any other officially issued certificates. The {authMethod} step takes {authDaysMin}–{authDaysMax} days and costs €{authFeeMin}–{authFeeMax} per document — and each document will also need a sworn German translation (€20–60 per page). The total authentication and translation budget for an average Studium file from {country} typically runs €300–800.
studium.p3: The Studienkolleg is a preparatory year required if your secondary school diploma does not directly qualify you for German university admission. Use the Anabin database (anabin.kmk.org) to check your qualification's status before applying. Applicants are also required to open a Sperrkonto (blocked account) holding €11,904 as proof of financial means — online providers such as Fintiba, Expatrio or Coracle open one within a few days. A German B2 language certificate (Goethe, telc, ÖSD, or TestDaF) is mandatory for German-taught programmes; English-taught programmes accept IELTS/TOEFL instead.
studium.p4: The total document count for a Studium visa from {country} is {totalDocs} items, and the estimated total cost (documents, authentication, translations, Sperrkonto setup, and visa fee) is €{totalCostMin}–{totalCostMax}. The realistic preparation timeline is {timelineMin}–{timelineMax} weeks. Start at least 6 months before your intended study start — German universities send admissions letters late, and apostille or legalization queues in {country} can run several weeks.

tourist.p1: Citizens of {country} need a Schengen C visa (also called a short-stay or tourist visa) to visit Germany and the broader Schengen Area. The Schengen C visa allows up to 90 days of stay in any 180-day rolling period and covers tourism, family visits, short business trips, and cultural events. The application is submitted at the German embassy, consulate, or an authorised visa centre (VFS Global or TLScontact) in {country}.
tourist.p2: The Schengen tourist visa fee is €{visaFee} as of 2024 (raised from €80 in June 2024 under the revised EU Visa Code). Children under 6 are exempt; children aged 6–12 pay €45. The fee is non-refundable even if the visa is refused. You will also pay any visa-centre service charges on top of the consular fee. In {country}, total application costs including insurance and document preparation typically range from €150 to €350.
tourist.p3: The strongest factor in a Schengen visa approval is demonstrating strong ties to your home country — proof that you intend to return. An employment letter granting you approved leave, a property deed, a business registration, or a student enrolment certificate all serve this purpose. Financial proof must show you can cover approximately €45–100 per day of your stay. Travel health insurance with a minimum coverage of €30,000 and valid for all Schengen countries is mandatory.
tourist.p4: Appointment wait times at the German mission or visa centre in {country} vary by season: expect {authDaysMin}–{authDaysMax} business days in off-peak periods and up to 8 weeks in summer. Processing after submission takes a maximum of 15 calendar days for straightforward applications (up to 30 days for complex cases, 45 days in exceptional circumstances). Multiple-entry visas valid for 1–5 years can be issued to frequent travellers with a clean travel history.

family_reunification.p1: Family reunification to Germany — bringing a spouse, minor children, or dependent parents to join a German resident — is regulated by §§27–36 of the AufenthG. Citizens of {country} applying to join a family member in Germany must obtain a national D-visa before arriving. The most common case is spousal reunion (Ehegattennachzug), which gives the spouse the right to work in Germany immediately upon arrival.
family_reunification.p2: The most distinctive requirement for spouses applying from {country} is the German A1 language certificate. Before a spousal reunion visa is issued, the applicant must demonstrate basic German-language proficiency at CEFR level A1 (Goethe-Zertifikat A1, telc Deutsch A1 or ÖSD Zertifikat A1). Exceptions exist if the sponsor holds a German Hochschulabschluss or has C1-level German, if the applicant is over 67, or if there is a proven hardship case. Document authentication from {country} uses {authMethod} and costs €{authFeeMin}–{authFeeMax} per document, adding {authDaysMin}–{authDaysMax} days.
family_reunification.p3: The sponsor (the person already in Germany) plays a central role: they must prove that their income is sufficient to support the reunited family without recourse to public funds. The required income threshold varies by Bundesland and household size but typically equals the Grundsicherung minimum plus 20%. The sponsor must also prove adequate housing — a minimum of 12 m² of living space per additional person is the benchmark used by most Ausländerbehörden. These documents (income proof, housing confirmation) must be sent to you in {country} before your visa appointment.
family_reunification.p4: From {country}, the full process — gathering documents, authentication ({authMethod}), A1 certificate, and the visa appointment — takes {timelineMin}–{timelineMax} weeks. The national D-visa fee is €{visaFee}. Once in Germany, the sponsored family member must register at the local Einwohnermeldeamt within two weeks and apply for a residence permit (Aufenthaltstitel) at the Ausländerbehörde. Spouses have the right to take up any employment immediately; children of school age are integrated into the public school system without additional permit requirements.

seoContent.noVisaEu: As a citizen of {country}, you benefit from the European Union's freedom of movement — one of the most significant rights in the EU legal order. You can live, work, study, or retire in Germany for any length of time without obtaining a visa, residence permit, or work permit. The only administrative step required is registering your address at the local Einwohnermeldeamt (Anmeldung) within two weeks of arrival, and enrolling in health insurance if you are employed.
seoContent.touristFree: Citizens of {country} are exempt from the Schengen C tourist visa under a bilateral visa-free agreement or EU/EEA freedom of movement. You may enter Germany and the Schengen Area for stays of up to 90 days in any 180-day period without any visa. For stays longer than 90 days — for Ausbildung, Studium, or family reunification — a national D-visa is required. The D-visa application is submitted at the German embassy or honorary consulate responsible for your residence in {country}.

ausbildung.q: How many documents do I need for the German Ausbildung visa from {country}?
ausbildung.a: A standard Ausbildung visa application from {country} requires {totalDocs} documents. The most critical are the signed Ausbildungsvertrag (training contract) from your German employer, a German B1/B2 language certificate, authenticated school diplomas and transcripts, and proof of financial means. Every document in a language other than German must be accompanied by a sworn German translation.

ausbildung.q: How long does it take to get a German Ausbildung visa from {country}?
ausbildung.a: The realistic end-to-end timeline from {country} is {timelineMin}–{timelineMax} weeks. The bottleneck is usually document authentication ({authMethod}: {authDaysMin}–{authDaysMax} days), followed by the visa appointment waiting time (often 4–12 weeks), and consulate processing (8–12 weeks without Vorab-Zustimmung, ~8 weeks with it). Start preparing at least 6 months before your training start date.

ausbildung.q: Does {country} require apostille or consular legalization for a German visa?
ausbildung.a: For German visa applications, {country} documents must undergo {authMethod}. {authMethodDetail} The cost is €{authFeeMin}–{authFeeMax} per document and the process takes {authDaysMin}–{authDaysMax} days. Plan this step first as it is the hardest to accelerate.

ausbildung.q: What is the German Ausbildung visa fee?
ausbildung.a: The national D-visa fee for Ausbildung is €{visaFee}, paid in cash or by card at your appointment. The fee is non-refundable if the visa is refused. Some German visa centres (TLScontact, VFS) charge an additional service fee of €20–40.

ausbildung.q: Do I need to speak German before applying for an Ausbildung visa from {country}?
ausbildung.a: Yes. Most Ausbildung visas require a minimum German B1 certificate (Goethe-Institut, telc or ÖSD). Many employers and some training sectors (healthcare, trades) require B2. Start your German classes early — the B1 exam takes 3–6 months of study from zero, and B2 takes a further 3–4 months. The certificate must not be older than 2 years at the time of your visa appointment.

ausbildung.q: Do I need a Sperrkonto for the Ausbildung visa from {country}?
ausbildung.a: It depends on your training salary. If your gross monthly salary is below approximately €934, you will likely need a Sperrkonto (blocked account) holding €11,904. Trainees with higher salaries or those whose German employer provides a Verpflichtungserklärung (financial guarantee) may be exempt. Confirm with the German mission in {country} as requirements vary.

studium.q: How many documents are required for a German Studium visa from {country}?
studium.a: A Studium visa application from {country} typically requires {totalDocs} documents, including: university admission letter (Zulassung), German B2 or TestDaF language certificate, Baccalauréat diploma and transcripts (authenticated and translated), higher-education diplomas (if applicable), proof of financial means (Sperrkonto at €11,904 or equivalent), and travel health insurance.

studium.q: How long does it take to get a Studium visa from {country}?
studium.a: From {country}, the realistic timeline is {timelineMin}–{timelineMax} weeks. The document authentication stage ({authMethod}: {authDaysMin}–{authDaysMax} days) and the university admission process (which can take 3–6 months via uni-assist or directly) are the longest steps. Apply to German universities a full year before your intended start date.

studium.q: What is the Sperrkonto and is it mandatory for students from {country}?
studium.a: The Sperrkonto is a blocked bank account holding €11,904 (as of 2026), which proves you can cover your living costs for the first year in Germany. The funds are released to you in monthly instalments of €992 after you arrive. It is mandatory for most Studium visa applicants from {country} unless you have an equivalent scholarship or a strong Verpflichtungserklärung. Set one up through Fintiba, Expatrio, or Coracle — they can open the account within a few business days.

studium.q: Do I need an APS certificate from {country} for a German Studium visa?
studium.a: APS (Akademische Prüfstelle) certificates are required for applicants from China, India, Vietnam, Mongolia, and Pakistan. For {country}, {apsDetail}. If required, apply for the APS early as processing takes 6–20 weeks and the certificate is mandatory before the German mission will process your visa.

studium.q: What does document authentication cost for students from {country}?
studium.a: For applicants from {country}, authentication uses {authMethod} and costs €{authFeeMin}–{authFeeMax} per document, taking {authDaysMin}–{authDaysMax} days. For a standard Studium file you will authenticate roughly 4–6 documents (diplomas, transcripts, birth certificate, police clearance). Add sworn translations at €20–60 per page. Total authentication and translation budget: typically €300–800 from {country}.

studium.q: Can I work in Germany while studying on a Studium visa?
studium.a: Yes. Students on a German Studium visa may work up to 120 full days or 240 half-days per year without needing a separate work permit. Hours above this limit require approval from the Ausländerbehörde and Bundesagentur für Arbeit. Student jobs (Werkstudent, Hiwi, or mini-job) are a common way to supplement living costs.

tourist.q: Do {country} citizens need a visa to visit Germany?
tourist.a: Yes, citizens of {country} need a Schengen C (tourist/short-stay) visa to enter Germany and all Schengen countries. The visa permits up to 90 days of stay in any 180-day period. The application is submitted at the German embassy, consulate, or an authorised visa centre (VFS Global, TLScontact) serving {country}.

tourist.q: What documents do I need for a German tourist visa from {country}?
tourist.a: A German Schengen tourist visa from {country} requires {totalDocs} documents: completed Schengen application form, valid passport (3+ months beyond trip), biometric photos (2×), travel health insurance (€30,000+ coverage), round-trip flight reservation, accommodation proof (hotel or invitation letter), bank statements showing sufficient funds (€45–100/day), and proof of ties to {country} such as an employment letter or property deed.

tourist.q: What is the German tourist visa fee for {country} citizens?
tourist.a: The standard Schengen C visa fee is €{visaFee} (revised June 2024). Children under 6 are free; children 6–12 pay €45. The fee is non-refundable. Additional visa-centre service fees (VFS/TLScontact) of €20–40 may apply. Total payment is made at the appointment — check with your local visa centre for accepted payment methods.

tourist.q: How long does it take to get a German tourist visa from {country}?
tourist.a: Standard processing is 15 calendar days from the date of application. It can extend to 30 days and exceptionally up to 45 days. Factor in the appointment wait at the visa centre: {authDaysMin}–{authDaysMax} days in normal periods, up to 8 weeks during summer peak season. Book your appointment as early as possible — at least 3 months before your planned travel date.

tourist.q: How much money do I need to show for a German tourist visa from {country}?
tourist.a: Germany requires proof of approximately €45–100 per day of your stay in the Schengen area. For a 14-day trip, that is roughly €630–1,400. Bank statements from the last 3 months are the standard evidence. If a family member or German host is sponsoring you, a Verpflichtungserklärung (financial guarantee, issued at a German Ausländerbehörde) can substitute for your own funds.

tourist.q: Can a Schengen tourist visa be extended or converted to a longer visa in Germany?
tourist.a: A Schengen C tourist visa cannot normally be extended beyond 90 days and cannot be converted into a national D-visa inside Germany. If you wish to stay longer — for Ausbildung, Studium, or family reasons — you must return to {country} and apply for the appropriate national D-visa through the German mission before re-entering Germany.

family_reunification.q: What documents do I need for a German family reunification visa from {country}?
family_reunification.a: A family reunification visa from {country} requires {totalDocs} documents across two sides: your documents (passport, birth certificate, marriage certificate, police clearance, German A1 certificate if joining a spouse, plus authenticated translations), and your sponsor's documents from Germany (copy of their Aufenthaltstitel, last 3 salary slips, tax assessment, and housing confirmation showing ≥12 m² per additional person).

family_reunification.q: Is the German A1 language certificate mandatory for family reunification from {country}?
family_reunification.a: Yes, for spousal reunification (Ehegattennachzug) from {country}, you must present a German A1 language certificate (Goethe-Zertifikat A1, telc Deutsch A1 or ÖSD Zertifikat A1) at your visa appointment. Exceptions: your sponsor holds a German Hochschulabschluss or has documented C1+ German, you are over 67, you have a recognised disability that prevents language learning, or a compelling hardship case exists. Children under 16 joining parents are exempt.

family_reunification.q: How long does family reunification from {country} take?
family_reunification.a: The full process — document collection, authentication ({authMethod}: {authDaysMin}–{authDaysMax} days), A1 certificate exam, and visa appointment — takes {timelineMin}–{timelineMax} weeks from {country}. The German mission is required to decide on a complete application within 3 months. Incomplete files are returned without a decision, restarting the clock.

family_reunification.q: How much income does the sponsor in Germany need for family reunification?
family_reunification.a: The sponsor must earn enough to support the family without public assistance. The threshold varies by Bundesland and family size: roughly €1,600–2,200 net per month for a couple, plus €300–400 per additional child. The sponsor submits the last 3 salary slips and a tax assessment (Steuerbescheid) to the German mission on your behalf. Self-employed sponsors can use profit-and-loss statements.

family_reunification.q: Can the spouse work in Germany after family reunification?
family_reunification.a: Yes. A spouse joining a German resident or EU/EEA national receives an Aufenthaltstitel (residence permit) that includes full, unrestricted work authorisation — no employer sponsorship needed. They may take up any employed or self-employed work immediately upon receiving their permit. Children of school age are automatically integrated into the public school system.

family_reunification.q: What authentication method does {country} use for family reunification documents?
family_reunification.a: Documents from {country} must be authenticated via {authMethod} for German visa purposes. {authMethodDetail} Authentication costs €{authFeeMin}–{authFeeMax} per document and takes {authDaysMin}–{authDaysMax} days. Every authenticated document must also be accompanied by a sworn German translation (€20–60 per page). Start the authentication process as early as possible — it is the step most applicants underestimate.

authMethodDetail.apostille: {country} is a member of the Hague Convention and Germany accepts its apostilles. Your documents are authenticated with an apostille stamp from the relevant national authority.
authMethodDetail.legalization: Despite being a Hague Convention member, Germany has formally objected to {country}'s accession. Full consular legalization via the German embassy or a chain of national authorities is therefore required — not an apostille.

apsDetail.required: an APS (Akademische Prüfstelle) certificate IS required. You must have your academic documents verified by the APS office before submitting your visa application.
apsDetail.notRequired: an APS certificate is NOT required. You can submit your authenticated academic documents directly in your visa file.

seoSection.title: Why a 60-second eligibility check matters before you book a consulate appointment
seoSection.intro:
This Ausbildung & Studium eligibility checker tells you in 60 seconds whether your current profile qualifies for a German visa — and exactly what you need to fix if not. It works for both apprenticeship (Ausbildung) and university (Studium) routes, applying the actual 2026 German consulate rules: minimum German level (B1 for Ausbildung, B2/C1 for Studium), recognised diploma, signed contract or admission letter, financial proof (Sperrkonto, salary, or sponsor), and proof of housing.

Most rejected visa applications fail on a single missable detail — language proof not accepted, contract not yet signed, Sperrkonto below the 2026 threshold of €11,904. The checker catches these before you spend money on a consulate appointment. The result page shows a clear green/orange/red verdict, the specific blockers in your profile, and the next concrete step for each one. It does not replace a real assessment by a specialist; for borderline cases or unusual profiles (gap year, prior visa refusal, dual citizenship), book a 30-minute consultation.
seoSection.faqTitle: Common questions about the eligibility check

faqs.q: How accurate is the result?
faqs.a: It applies the published German consulate criteria for international applicants in 2026. It catches the common rejection patterns (around 85% of cases) but cannot factor in subjective consular judgment. For complex profiles, book a consultation.

faqs.q: Which visa types does this cover?
faqs.a: Both the Ausbildung visa (§16a AufenthG) and the Studium visa (§16b AufenthG). The Jobseeker visa and Skilled Worker visa use different rules — those are not covered by this tool yet.

faqs.q: Is my data saved?
faqs.a: No. The check runs entirely in your browser. We do not see what you enter, and nothing is sent to our servers.

german_level_ausbildung.b2_strong: B2 is well above the legal B1 minimum. You'll have a clear advantage in interviews and the visa officer's first read. No further German action needed for the visa step.
german_level_ausbildung.b1_min: B1 is the legal minimum for the Ausbildung visa — you're cleared. To stand out in interviews, working toward B2 in your free time pays off; most employers prefer it.
german_level_ausbildung.a2_close: A2 is one CEFR level below the B1 minimum. Plan 4–6 months of intensive German (4h/day at a Goethe-Institut or telc-licensed school) to reach B1 and become visa-eligible.
german_level_ausbildung.below: B1 is the legal minimum for the Ausbildung visa. Realistic plan: 4–6 months of intensive study per CEFR level (a Goethe-Institut, telc-licensed school, or online), so 8–14 months from A0/A1 to B1. Intensive courses (4 hours/day) get you there fastest.

german_level_studium.c1_strong: C1 covers every German university requirement, including TestDaF and DSH-2. You are fully set on the language front.
german_level_studium.b2_min: B2 is the standard university requirement, accepted by most programs. A few selective tracks (medicine, top-tier humanities) ask for C1 / TestDaF 4 / DSH-2 — verify on your target university's page.
german_level_studium.b1_close: About 30% of German universities accept B1 with conditional admission — you commit to reaching C1 during your studies. The other 70% require B2 or higher upfront. Apply to several universities to maximise your chances.
german_level_studium.below: Most Studium programs require B2 minimum. Realistic plan: 8–14 months of intensive German (Goethe Institut, telc, or DSH-Vorbereitungskurs) to reach B2 from A0/A1. Alternative: target English-taught Master programs and tick the "English program" toggle above.
german_level_studium.english_program: For an English-taught program, A1 German is often enough — some programs accept any level. You'll still want to pick up German for daily life, but it doesn't block the visa.
german_level_studium.english_program_a1: Even for a fully English program, A1 German makes Anmeldung, banking, and daily life much smoother in your first months.

education_ausbildung.no_bac: A few Ausbildungen accept candidates without a Bac (Pflegehelfer in healthcare, some retail and gastronomy positions), but your options narrow significantly. Completing the Bac first is strongly recommended — opens roughly 5× more positions.
education_ausbildung.bac_ok: Your Bac qualifies you for any of the 1,100+ Ausbildung positions on our platform — IT, healthcare, engineering, hospitality, automotive, and more.

education_studium_bachelor.no_bac: A Bac (or a recognised equivalent) is non-negotiable for Bachelor admission in Germany. If you have a Bac+2 or vocational diploma instead, check the Anabin database to see how it maps to the German system.
education_studium_bachelor.bac_ok: Your Bac qualifies you for Bachelor admission in Germany — provided your average meets the threshold (see Bac average rule).

education_studium_master.licence_ok: Your Licence (Bac+3) or Master (Bac+5) is the right starting level for a German Master program. Check Anabin to confirm your home university is listed as H+ (recognised).
education_studium_master.bac_plus_2: Bac+2 is below the German Master standard (180 ECTS / 3-year Licence). Either complete a 3rd year of your degree in your home country, or apply for Bachelor entry in Germany with credit recognition for what you have already done.
education_studium_master.below: A 3-year Licence (Bac+3, 180 ECTS) is the minimum for German Master admission. Path forward: complete your degree in your home country, or do a Bachelor in Germany first.

bac_grade_studium.tres_bien: Bac average ≥ 14/20 (mention 'Bien' or 'Très Bien') qualifies you for direct Bachelor admission in Germany. Strongest asset for your application file.
bac_grade_studium.assez_bien: Bac average 12–13.99 (mention 'Assez Bien') usually requires a Studienkolleg before direct Bachelor admission. Studienkolleg is a 1-year preparatory program in Germany — apply via your target university, B1 German minimum.
bac_grade_studium.passable: Bac average 10–11.99 typically does not qualify for German universities, even via Studienkolleg. Strongly consider the Ausbildung path instead — same outcome (career in Germany) without the academic threshold.
bac_grade_studium.failing: A Bac average below 10 doesn't qualify for German universities. The Ausbildung path is the better route for you — German employers value motivation and concrete skills more than Bac grades.

contract_ausbildung.have: You hold the visa-blocker. Make sure your contract specifies start date, monthly salary (≥ €934 ideally), 3-year training duration, and the IHK or HWK registration number.
contract_ausbildung.missing: You need a signed Ausbildungsvertrag from a German employer registered with IHK or HWK before you can apply for the visa. Start with our 1,100+ open Ausbildung positions, then apply with a German CV (Lebenslauf) and motivation letter (Anschreiben). Asking the employer for a Vorab-Zustimmung cuts visa wait by 6 months.

admission_studium.have: Zulassung in hand — the visa-blocker is resolved. Carry the original plus 2 photocopies in your visa application file.
admission_studium.missing: Apply via Uni-Assist (uni-assist.de) for most universities, or directly for the rest. Deadlines: 15 July for the Winter semester, 15 January for Summer. Apply at least 4 months before each deadline — Uni-Assist's processing alone takes 4–6 weeks.

aps_studium.have: APS certificate is in hand — the most time-consuming Studium step is done.
aps_studium.missing: APS is required for applicants from some countries (China, India, Vietnam, Pakistan…). Apply at the APS office for your country — processing takes 6–20 weeks and blocks every other Studium step. Bring all your transcripts since secondary school.

financial_proof.sperrkonto: Sperrkonto is the gold standard. Most international applicants use Fintiba, Expatrio, or Coracle (€89 setup + €11,904 deposit). The deposit is returned to you in 12 monthly instalments after arrival — it is not a fee.
financial_proof.sponsor: Verpflichtungserklärung accepted. Your sponsor must show ≥ €1,200 net monthly income (after tax), be willing to take legal liability, and sign at their local Ausländerbehörde. ~€29 fee paid by the sponsor.
financial_proof.salary_ausbildung: Your Ausbildung salary covers the visa minimum if it is ≥ €934/month after typical deductions. If your contract shows less, add a small Sperrkonto to bridge the gap.
financial_proof.family: Family support letters alone are weak evidence — they almost always trigger a request for additional proof. Strongly recommend pairing with a Sperrkonto (€11,904 from family savings, returned to you on arrival).
financial_proof.need_help: You need one of three: Sperrkonto (€11,904 from any source), Verpflichtungserklärung from a German sponsor, or an Ausbildung salary ≥ €934/month. Without one, the visa is rejected automatically. Book a consultation to find the best route for your situation.
financial_proof.studium_no_salary: For Studium you cannot rely on a future part-time student job as financial proof — you do not have it yet. Required: Sperrkonto €11,904 OR Verpflichtungserklärung from a German sponsor.
financial_proof.unclear: Lock in your financial proof before applying. Standard route: Sperrkonto via Fintiba / Expatrio / Coracle (~€89 setup + €11,904 deposit, returned to you in monthly instalments after arrival).

passport.valid: Your passport meets the validity requirement. Make sure it stays valid for at least 6 months past your visa expiry — most embassies require this.
passport.expiring: Your passport must be valid for at least 12 months at the time of your visa appointment. Renew with your country's passport authority — plan ahead, it can take weeks.

clean_record.clean: A clean police-clearance certificate is fine. It usually takes a few days to a few weeks to obtain and must be issued within 3 months of your visa appointment.
clean_record.case_by_case: Each case is reviewed individually. Minor traffic offenses or old fines are usually fine. Serious convictions (violence, drugs, fraud) can block the visa — book a confidential consultation before applying.

age_ausbildung.young: Ideal age range. Most Ausbildung employers prefer candidates under 30 for the 3-year commitment. You will have the widest choice of positions.
age_ausbildung.mid: 31–35 is well within range — no legal issue, just slightly less common. Healthcare, hospitality, and IT are particularly age-flexible sectors.
age_ausbildung.older: 36–40 is possible but more selective. Target sectors that value experience: healthcare (Pflegefachmann/frau), retail management, hospitality, and skilled trades. Your professional experience matters more than your age here.
age_ausbildung.much_older: Possible but rare. Best sectors at 40+: healthcare (Pflegefachmann/frau especially welcomed), gastronomy, and skilled trades where employers value mature, reliable workers. Position your CV around your professional experience, not the academic angle.

interviewPrep.title: Master your German Ausbildung interview
interviewPrep.subtitle: 15 of the most-asked questions, with sample answers in German plus the "why this is asked" and what to say (and avoid).
interviewPrep.lockedTitle: Log in to unlock the rest
interviewPrep.lockedBody: The first 3 questions are free. Create a free account to access all 15 questions, sample answers, and tips.
interviewPrep.ctaSub: Book a 1-hour consultation. We run a real Vorstellungsgespräch in German, score you, and give you concrete fixes — €20.

tell_about_yourself.why: The opener. Recruiters use it to gauge your German fluency, your structure, and whether you can present yourself confidently in 60–90 seconds.
tell_about_yourself.doSay: Stick to a 3-part structure: who you are (name, age, where from) → what you bring (Bac, German level, motivation) → why this Ausbildung. Stay under 90 seconds.
tell_about_yourself.dontSay: Don't recite your whole CV. Don't talk about hobbies for more than one sentence. Don't mention salary, holidays, or family problems.

why_us.translation: Why did you apply to us?
why_us.why: Tests whether you researched the company. The wrong answer ("you have a good reputation") signals a copy-paste application.
why_us.doSay: Cite 2 specific things from their website / press / LinkedIn — a product line, training program, location, recent project. Connect them to your goals.
why_us.dontSay: Don't say "I just need any Ausbildung". Don't bash competitors. Don't pretend you know things you don't — research before the call.

why_germany.translation: Why do you want to come to Germany?
why_germany.why: Tests whether your motivation is real and project-based — or whether Germany is just an "exit" from your home country. Recruiters reject candidates who sound like they'll leave once they have the visa.
why_germany.doSay: Give 3 reasons: dual training system, sector demand & job stability, the work culture (precision, punctuality). Frame it as a career project, not an escape.
why_germany.dontSay: Don't mention money, weather, or "Europe is better". Don't criticise your home country. Don't make it sound like a temporary plan.

strengths_weaknesses.translation: What are your strengths and weaknesses?
strengths_weaknesses.why: Classic trap. Strengths must be relevant, weaknesses must be real but improvable — fake humility ("I work too hard") gets seen instantly.
strengths_weaknesses.doSay: Pick 1–2 strengths tied to the job (reliability, learning speed, languages). For weakness: pick a real one, then explain how you actively manage it.
strengths_weaknesses.dontSay: Don't say you have no weaknesses. Don't claim "perfectionism" — it's the most overused fake answer. Don't reveal a deal-breaker (e.g. bad with deadlines).

mistake.translation: Tell me about a mistake you made.
mistake.why: Tests honesty, self-awareness, and ability to learn. The wrong answer ("I never make mistakes") is an instant disqualifier.
mistake.doSay: Pick a real, low-stakes mistake. Use the structure: what happened → what I did to fix it → what I learned and now do differently.
mistake.dontSay: Don't say you've never made a mistake. Don't blame others. Don't pick something catastrophic (lost a major client) or something trivial (forgot to refill the printer).

what_sets_you_apart.translation: What sets you apart from other applicants?
what_sets_you_apart.why: Your sales pitch. Other international candidates have similar profiles — what's your edge?
what_sets_you_apart.doSay: Pick 3 concrete differentiators: languages (AR/FR/DE), independence (organised your own migration), conscious career choice. Be specific, not generic.
what_sets_you_apart.dontSay: Don't say "I'm motivated and hard-working" — every candidate says that. Don't criticise other candidates. Don't list 10 qualities — pick 3.

stress.why: Tests your work style under pressure. They want to know whether you'll cope when an Ausbildung deadline collides with the Berufsschule exam.
stress.doSay: Describe a method: prioritise → tackle one task at a time → communicate early if a deadline slips. Frame stress as a signal, not a problem.
stress.dontSay: Don't say "I don't get stressed" — unrealistic. Don't describe panicking, working all night, or skipping breaks. Don't blame the workload.

criticism.translation: How do you react to criticism?
criticism.why: Tests teachability — the single most important quality in an Auszubildender. They want a learner, not someone who argues.
criticism.doSay: Describe a process: listen → ask clarifying questions → identify concrete next actions. Show that you separate the message from the messenger.
criticism.dontSay: Don't say "criticism doesn't affect me" — sounds defensive. Don't describe arguing back. Don't complain about a previous boss.

team_or_alone.translation: Do you prefer working alone or in a team?
team_or_alone.why: Tests fit. Most Ausbildung roles are team-heavy, but Berufsschule and exam prep are solo. They want someone who can do both.
team_or_alone.doSay: Say "both, depending on the task". Give one example each: team for collaborative learning, solo for focused execution. Show self-awareness.
team_or_alone.dontSay: Don't pick only one. Don't say "I'm a lone wolf". Don't say "I love working in teams" without explaining when solo work matters too.

overtime.translation: Would you be willing to work weekends or more than 40 hours?
overtime.why: A loyalty test, but also a legal trap. German Ausbildung law caps your hours — saying "yes always" sounds naive, "no never" sounds lazy.
overtime.doSay: Yes when there's a peak load or the team needs it. But also note: chronic overtime usually signals an organisation problem worth fixing together.
overtime.dontSay: Don't say "absolutely whenever". Don't cite legal limits aggressively (the §17 BBiG). Don't complain about pay.

five_years.translation: Where do you see yourself in five years?
five_years.why: Tests planning ability and loyalty. They want to know if you'll stay after the Ausbildung — replacing an Azubi is expensive.
five_years.doSay: Finished Ausbildung, 1–2 years of practice ideally with them, specialised in [concrete area], possibly Meister/Techniker/Fachwirt. Anchor your future at the company.
five_years.dontSay: Don't mention going back home. Don't mention switching companies. Don't say "I don't know" or "self-employed" — both signal flight risk.

why_this_field.translation: Why did you choose this field?
why_this_field.why: Tests authenticity. Random Ausbildung choices ("it was available") get rejected — they want a story showing you understand the profession.
why_this_field.doSay: Three layers: a personal story or experience → research you did (LinkedIn, YouTube, blogs) → the sector's future stability. Show genuine interest.
why_this_field.dontSay: Don't say "for the visa". Don't say "I had no other choice". Don't list random reasons — tell a coherent story.

salary.why: A trap — naming a number too high gets you rejected, too low signals lack of self-worth. For Ausbildung, the answer is mostly fixed by tariff.
salary.doSay: For Ausbildung: accept the tariff salary. State that you've seen typical year-1 ranges (€800–1200 brutto depending on sector) and prioritise quality of training.
salary.dontSay: Don't name a high number. Don't pretend money doesn't matter. Don't ask about salary in the first 30 minutes of the interview.

relocate.why: Easy question, but tests practical readiness. They want to hear that you've already thought through housing, transport, and cost of living.
relocate.doSay: Yes — relocation is part of the plan. Mention you've already researched the city (neighbourhoods, transport, costs). Show flexibility.
relocate.dontSay: Don't say "only if I can stay near my family". Don't hesitate. Don't ask whether the company helps with housing in the same answer.

questions_for_us.translation: Do you have any questions for us?
questions_for_us.why: The most underestimated question. "No, none" signals lack of preparation and interest. Use this to demonstrate research and fit.
questions_for_us.doSay: Have 3 questions ready: about a typical first month, the qualities of successful past Auszubildende, the post-Ausbildung retention rate. Show you're thinking long-term.
questions_for_us.dontSay: Don't say "no questions". Don't ask only about salary, holidays, or perks. Don't ask things you could find on the website.

studium.metaTitle: Student Visa Germany for internationals — Studium D-Visa Guide 2026
studium.metaDesc: Step-by-step student visa guide (§16b AufenthG) for international students applying through their German visa centre — documents, costs, timeline, common rejections.
studium.title: German student visa for internationals, step by step
studium.subtitle: Real procedure under §16b AufenthG. Apply at your country's German visa centre. Below: every step, every document, every cost — with EUR estimates and country-aware tips that no generic guide gives you.
studium.finalCtaTitle: Want a specialist to review your visa file?
studium.finalCtaSub: Most rejections are preventable. A 1-hour call with a specialist who reads German consulate rejection patterns daily — €20, in your language.

aps.title: 1. Get your APS certificate (if it applies to your country)
aps.desc: The Akademische Prüfstelle verifies your secondary-school and tertiary diplomas. Required for applicants from some countries (China, India, Vietnam, Pakistan, Mongolia…); skip this step if APS doesn't apply to you. Apply online at aps.diplo.de.

language.title: 2. Reach the required German level
language.desc: Most German-language Bachelor programs need C1 (TestDaF/DSH). English-taught programs need C1 English (IELTS 6.5+ / TOEFL 90+). A Goethe-Institut in your country is the standard test centre.

apply_uni.title: 3. Apply to universities and get an admission letter
apply_uni.desc: Use uni-assist for most universities. Deadlines: 15 July (winter) / 15 January (summer). The Zulassungsbescheid (admission letter) is the document the consulate needs.

sperrkonto.title: 4. Open a Sperrkonto (blocked account) with €11,904
sperrkonto.desc: For 2026: €11,904 = €992/month for 12 months. Open with Fintiba, Expatrio, or Coracle (all accept international applicants). The bank certificate proves you can fund yourself.

insurance.title: 5. Get expat health insurance for the visa
insurance.desc: Travel/expat insurance valid the day you arrive in Germany. Mawista, Care Concept or DR-WALTER are the cheapest accepted ones (~€30–60/month). You'll switch to public insurance once enrolled.

apostille.title: 6. Authenticate + sworn-translate your diplomas
apostille.desc: Authenticate your secondary-school diploma, transcripts and birth certificate — apostille for Hague-Convention countries, otherwise consular legalization. Then have them translated into German by a sworn/certified translator.

tls_appt.title: 7. Book your visa-centre appointment
tls_appt.desc: Online at your country's German visa-centre portal (TLScontact, VFS Global or iDATA). Slots are scarce — book as soon as you have your admission letter. Take a screenshot of the confirmation. Cancellation fees are real.

submit.title: 8. Submit your file at the visa centre
submit.desc: Bring originals + 2 copies of every document, in the order on the visa centre's checklist. Pay the €75 visa fee on site in local currency (cash or card). Biometric photos and fingerprints are taken.

decision.title: 9. Wait for the German consulate's decision
decision.desc: The visa centre only collects — the actual decision is made by the German mission responsible for your region. They may contact your German university for additional checks.

pickup.title: 10. Pick up your passport with the visa
pickup.desc: The visa centre emails you when ready. Bring your visa-centre receipt and ID. The visa stuck in your passport is valid 3–6 months — enter Germany within that window, then convert to a residence permit.

passport.title: Valid passport
passport.desc: Valid for at least 12 months from your visa appointment date. At least 2 blank pages.
passport.tip: If your passport expires within 18 months, renew it BEFORE booking the visa-centre appointment — the new passport number must match the application.

photos.title: Biometric photos (2)
photos.desc: German biometric format: 35×45 mm, white background, no glasses, no smile, taken within the last 6 months.
photos.tip: Most photo studios know the German biometric format — ask for a "German visa photo". Avoid smiling, glasses and shadows.

aps_certificate.title: APS Certificate (Akademische Prüfstelle)
aps_certificate.desc: Verification of your foreign diplomas, required for applicants from some countries (China, India, Vietnam, Pakistan…). Apply online at aps.diplo.de if APS applies to you.
aps_certificate.tip: Where APS applies, your file is rejected without it. Apply 3–4 months before your visa-centre appointment. Fee ~€250, valid for life.

admission_letter.title: Admission letter (Zulassungsbescheid)
admission_letter.desc: Official admission letter from your German university. Conditional admission (Zulassung mit Auflage) is also accepted but reduces visa chances.
admission_letter.tip: Get the unconditional Zulassung if you can. Save both the PDF and the printed signed version. Some unis email a digital signature only — print it anyway.

sperrkonto_proof.title: Sperrkonto (blocked account) proof
sperrkonto_proof.desc: Account opened at Fintiba/Expatrio/Coracle with €11,904 (2026 amount) for 12 months coverage. The bank issues a Sperrkonto certificate.
sperrkonto_proof.tip: Fintiba is the most common — accepts international SWIFT transfers from most banks. Allow ~2 weeks for the transfer to clear.

health_insurance.title: Travel/expat health insurance
health_insurance.desc: Coverage valid from your planned arrival date until enrolment in public German insurance. Minimum €30,000 coverage required.
health_insurance.tip: Mawista Student VISUM is the cheapest commonly accepted (~€33/month). Buy it AFTER your visa is approved if cash is tight; otherwise buy before the appointment.

language_cert.title: German or English language certificate
language_cert.desc: For German programs: TestDaF (TDN 4×4) or DSH 2 or telc Hochschule. For English programs: IELTS 6.5+ or TOEFL 90+. Goethe certificates are accepted as language proof for Studienkolleg.
language_cert.tip: TestDaF is offered several times a year at Goethe-Institut test centres. Register ~8 weeks ahead — slots fill fast before the autumn intake.

bac_diploma.title: Secondary-school diploma (e.g. Baccalauréat / Abitur)
bac_diploma.desc: Original + authentication (apostille or consular legalization) + sworn German translation. Some missions also want the full transcript.
bac_diploma.tip: Your diploma should show your final average/grade. If it doesn't, request an official duplicate from the issuing authority — usually 1–2 weeks.

transcripts.title: Higher-education transcripts (if applicable)
transcripts.desc: For applicants who completed any higher education — all year-by-year transcripts, authenticated and sworn-translated.
transcripts.tip: Ask for the complete, final transcript (not just year-by-year extracts), plus an official attestation for any program you didn't finish.

birth_certificate.title: Birth certificate (≤ 3 months old)
birth_certificate.desc: Issued within the 3 months before your visa-centre appointment. Authenticated (apostille or consular legalization) and translated into German by a sworn translator.
birth_certificate.tip: From your local civil registry. Order ~4 copies: 1 for the consulate, 1 for the translator, 1 spare, 1 for German bureaucracy after arrival.

cv.title: CV in tabular German format
cv.desc: Lebenslauf in German listing your studies and any work experience, photo top-right, signed at the bottom.
cv.tip: Use our free CV Builder — it outputs the German format with the right fields, sections, and date layout. Sign it in blue ink.

motivation_letter.title: Motivation letter in German
motivation_letter.desc: 1 page minimum, explaining: why this program, why this university, why Germany, your post-graduation plan back home or career goals.
motivation_letter.tip: The "back home" angle is critical to overcome doubt-of-return rejections. Be specific about what you'll do AFTER graduation.

criminal_record.title: Police clearance — clean criminal record
criminal_record.desc: Issued by your country's police/judicial authority, ≤ 3 months old, authenticated, translated.
criminal_record.tip: Processing time varies by country — usually a few days. Request it early so it's still within the 3-month window at your appointment.

application_form.title: VIDEX application form
application_form.desc: Completed online at videx-national.diplo.de, printed, signed (twice — once at the bottom, once on the data-protection page).
application_form.tip: Use the latest VIDEX version (2024+). Old PDFs are rejected. Print it AFTER booking your visa-centre appointment so the date matches.

declaration_truth.title: Declaration of truthful information (§54 AufenthG)
declaration_truth.desc: Signed declaration that all info in the file is correct. Form provided by the consulate.
declaration_truth.tip: Lying here is a permanent ban from the Schengen area. Even small omissions get caught at the consulate-AusländerBehörde cross-check.

weak_finances.title: Insufficient or doubtful financial proof
weak_finances.desc: The Sperrkonto is short of €11,904, OR the source of the deposit is unclear (e.g. unexplained transfer from a third party).
weak_finances.fix: Deposit the full amount. If the money came from family, attach a notarised parental support letter (déclaration de prise en charge) translated into German.

doubt_return.title: Doubt about return home after studies
doubt_return.desc: The consulate suspects the candidate plans to overstay. Triggers: vague motivation letter, no family ties, no career plan, age above program norm.
doubt_return.fix: Motivation letter must explicitly state your post-graduation plan back home or your career thesis. Include your family ties at home (parents, siblings).

weak_motivation.title: Vague or copy-paste motivation letter
weak_motivation.desc: Generic phrases ("Germany has the best universities"), no specifics on the program/professor/lab, no link to a real need back home.
weak_motivation.fix: Mention 2 specific professors/labs/courses from your program, and explain how the diploma will translate into a career back home or internationally.

language_below.title: Language certificate below the program threshold
language_below.desc: Bringing TestDaF TDN 3 to a TDN 4-required program, or B2 to a C1 program. Auto-rejection.
language_below.fix: Re-take the test. Goethe-Institut test centres offer TestDaF several times a year. If your appointment is close, request to postpone — better than a rejection on file.

fake_documents.title: Fake or altered documents
fake_documents.desc: Forged diplomas, fake bank statements, false employer attestations. The consulate cross-checks with authorities in your country.
fake_documents.fix: Never. Detection is a Schengen-wide ban. If a document is unfavourable, address it head-on in the motivation letter — the consulate respects honesty.

no_aps.title: Missing or expired APS certificate
no_aps.desc: No APS = no review of your file. APS doesn't expire but you must show the original.
no_aps.fix: Apply at aps.diplo.de 4 months before your visa-centre appointment. Bring both the PDF and the original signed certificate to the appointment.

incomplete_file.title: Incomplete or disordered file
incomplete_file.desc: Missing one document, or out-of-order, or photocopies in place of originals. The consulate doesn't pick the missing piece up — they reject the whole file.
incomplete_file.fix: Use the visa centre's exact checklist. Order: passport, photos, application form, then APS, admission, finances, language, education, civil status. Tab-divide.

health_insurance.title: Insurance not accepted by the consulate
health_insurance.desc: Some travel insurances aren't recognised. Coverage period also matters: must cover from arrival until enrolment.
health_insurance.fix: Use Mawista, Care Concept, or DR-WALTER — all explicitly accepted. Coverage at least €30,000, valid from your travel date.

apostille_missing.title: Documents not apostilled or not properly translated
apostille_missing.desc: Diploma without apostille/legalization, or translation by a non-sworn translator. The consulate requires both.
apostille_missing.fix: Authenticate via your country's competent authority (apostille or consular legalization). Use a sworn translator on the official list.

ausbildung.metaTitle: Ausbildung Visa Germany for internationals — D-Visa Vocational 2026
ausbildung.metaDesc: Step-by-step Ausbildung visa guide (§16a AufenthG) for international applicants — documents, costs, BA-ZAV approval, timeline, common rejections.
ausbildung.title: German Ausbildung visa for internationals, step by step
ausbildung.subtitle: Real procedure under §16a AufenthG. The Ausbildung visa requires both a contract AND BA-ZAV approval. Below: every step, every document, every cost — with EUR estimates and country-aware tips.
ausbildung.finalCtaTitle: Want a specialist to check your Ausbildung file?
ausbildung.finalCtaSub: Visa officers focus on language proof and contract authenticity for Ausbildung. A 1-hour call with someone who reviews these files weekly — €20, in your language.

language_b1.title: 1. Reach German B1 (minimum)
language_b1.desc: B1 is the minimum for most Ausbildungen. Some healthcare and hospitality positions accept A2 entry with B1 by Berufsschule. Get certified at a Goethe-Institut in your country.

find_employer.title: 2. Find an employer with an Ausbildungsplatz
find_employer.desc: Apply via Make-it-in-Germany, BIBB, IHK portals, Hwk, or directly to companies. Categories with the highest acceptance: healthcare (Pflege), hospitality (Hotelfach), trades (Metall/Elektro), IT, logistics.

sign_contract.title: 3. Sign the Ausbildungsvertrag
sign_contract.desc: A 3-year contract with monthly Vergütung (800–1,400 € gross). The contract must be officially registered with IHK or Hwk before you submit the visa file.

finances.title: 4. Prove you can finance the gap
finances.desc: Your salary covers most needs but the consulate often wants proof for the first 3 months. Either a Sperrkonto (~6,000 €) OR a parental support letter (Verpflichtungserklärung) from a relative in Germany.

insurance.title: 5. Get health insurance for arrival
insurance.desc: Same as Studium: travel insurance from arrival until you join the public system through your employer. Mawista, Care Concept, DR-WALTER (~30–60 €/month).

apostille.title: 6. Authenticate + sworn-translate diplomas
apostille.desc: Your secondary-school diploma (or equivalent) + birth certificate + criminal record — authenticated (apostille for Hague-Convention countries, otherwise consular legalization). Then sworn translation into German.

tls_appt.title: 7. Book the visa-centre appointment
tls_appt.desc: Same as Studium: your country's German visa-centre portal. Indicate "Ausbildung / Berufsausbildung" in the visa type.

submit.title: 8. Submit your file at the visa centre
submit.desc: Originals + 2 copies of every document. Pay 75 € on site in local currency. Biometric photos and fingerprints.

ba_zav.title: 9. BA-ZAV (Bundesagentur für Arbeit) approval
ba_zav.desc: For Ausbildung the German Federal Employment Agency must also approve. Done in parallel with consulate review. Required check: contract terms match labour law (no exploitation).

decision.title: 10. Final decision
decision.desc: Once both BA-ZAV and the consulate clear the file, the visa is issued. The Konsulat is the decision authority.

pickup.title: 11. Pick up your passport
pickup.desc: The visa centre emails when ready. Visa is valid 3–6 months — enter Germany within that window. Convert to Aufenthaltserlaubnis at the local Ausländerbehörde within 90 days of arrival.

passport.title: Valid passport
passport.desc: Valid for at least 12 months from your visa appointment. At least 2 blank pages.
passport.tip: Keep your old passport too — German bureaucracy sometimes asks for previous travel history.

photos.title: Biometric photos (2)
photos.desc: German biometric format: 35×45 mm, white background.
photos.tip: Same studios as for Studium. Allow extras — your Anmeldung in Germany will need 2 more.

ausbildung_contract.title: Ausbildungsvertrag (registered)
ausbildung_contract.desc: Signed by employer + IHK/Hwk-stamped contract. Must mention salary, duration (3 years), Berufsschule, and your role.
ausbildung_contract.tip: Without IHK/Hwk registration, the visa is rejected. Your employer's HR knows the process; if they don't, that's a red flag.

language_cert.title: German language certificate (B1 minimum)
language_cert.desc: Goethe B1, telc B1, or ÖSD B1. Some healthcare/hospitality positions accept A2 with B1 by start.
language_cert.tip: Goethe-Institut centres offer B1 regularly. Cost ~155 €. Register ~6 weeks ahead — slots fill before the main intakes.

finances_proof.title: Financial proof for first 3 months
finances_proof.desc: Either a Sperrkonto with ~6,000 €, OR a Verpflichtungserklärung (formal sponsorship from a relative in Germany), OR salary advance proof from employer.
finances_proof.tip: If you have a relative in Germany with stable income, the Verpflichtungserklärung at their local Ausländerbehörde is faster and cheaper than a Sperrkonto.

health_insurance.title: Travel/expat health insurance
health_insurance.desc: Coverage from arrival until your employer registers you in the public health system (~2–4 weeks).
health_insurance.tip: Mawista, Care Concept, DR-WALTER. ~30 €/month is enough.

school_diploma.title: Secondary-school diploma or equivalent
school_diploma.desc: Original + authentication + sworn translation. Some Ausbildungen don't require a school-leaving diploma (e.g. handwerk) but the consulate still wants your highest diploma.
school_diploma.tip: A vocational/technical secondary qualification is often even better than an academic diploma for technical Ausbildungen — request a certified copy from your training centre.

birth_certificate.title: Birth certificate (≤ 3 months)
birth_certificate.desc: Authenticated and translated, same as Studium.
birth_certificate.tip: From your local civil registry. ~4 copies recommended.

cv.title: CV in German
cv.desc: Lebenslauf with your studies and any work experience.
cv.tip: Use our free CV Builder. For Ausbildung, prioritise any internship or part-time job — even informal — to show work-readiness.

motivation_letter.title: Motivation letter in German
motivation_letter.desc: Why this Beruf, why this employer, why Germany. Mention your German learning journey and post-Ausbildung plan.
motivation_letter.tip: For Ausbildung, the consulate wants to see commitment. Mention you'll stay with the employer after Ausbildung if possible.

criminal_record.title: Police clearance
criminal_record.desc: Your country's police/judicial authority, ≤ 3 months, authenticated, translated.
criminal_record.tip: Processing time varies by country — usually a few days. Request it early.

application_form.title: VIDEX application form
application_form.tip: Indicate "Berufsausbildung" as visa purpose. Use latest VIDEX (2024+).

declaration_truth.title: Declaration of truth (§54 AufenthG)
declaration_truth.desc: Signed declaration that file info is correct.

professional_recognition.title: Professional qualification recognition (if applicable)
professional_recognition.desc: For regulated professions (e.g. nursing, electrician), Anerkennung from the Anerkennungsbescheid is needed before or during the Ausbildung.
professional_recognition.tip: Most simple Ausbildungen don't need this. Healthcare: yes, request via the Anerkennung-Finder website.

sperrkonto_block.label: Sperrkonto (~6,000 € — 3 months coverage, optional if Verpflichtungserklärung)

weak_finances.title: Financial proof for the gap before first paycheck
weak_finances.desc: No Sperrkonto, no Verpflichtungserklärung, and Ausbildung salary alone doesn't reassure for the first 1–3 months.
weak_finances.fix: Sperrkonto with 6,000 € OR Verpflichtungserklärung from a German-resident relative OR an employer letter confirming a salary advance.

language_below.title: German below B1
language_below.desc: Bringing A2 to a B1-required Ausbildung. Auto-rejection (or contingent).
language_below.fix: Re-take B1 at Goethe — 6 sessions per year. If your appointment is close, postpone — better than a "language insufficient" stamp.

contract_doubts.title: Doubts about the Ausbildung contract
contract_doubts.desc: Contract not registered with IHK/Hwk, salary below tariff (less than €730 in 2026), employer not previously known to BA-ZAV.
contract_doubts.fix: Verify your contract is IHK/Hwk-registered. If salary is below tariff, ask your employer to fix it. Reputable employers know.

doubt_return.title: Doubt the candidate plans to stay illegally
doubt_return.desc: Triggers: weak family ties, age outside Ausbildung norm (35+), motivation letter saying "I want to stay in Germany forever".
doubt_return.fix: Reframe motivation as "I want to learn this profession, then evaluate". Mention family ties at home. Don't bury the post-Ausbildung plan.

fake_documents.title: Fake/altered documents
fake_documents.desc: Fake employer attestation, fake bank statements, fake school diplomas.

incomplete_file.title: Incomplete or disordered file
incomplete_file.desc: Missing 1 document, or photocopies in place of originals.
incomplete_file.fix: Use the visa centre's exact checklist. Tab-divide.

apostille_missing.title: Documents not apostilled or not properly translated
apostille_missing.desc: Diploma without apostille/legalization, or non-sworn translation.
apostille_missing.fix: Authenticate via your country's competent authority (apostille or consular legalization). Sworn translator only.

school_diploma.title: Inadequate school diploma
school_diploma.desc: For some Ausbildungen, no Bac and no Brevet shown.
school_diploma.fix: Even partial schooling counts. Provide whatever you have. CAP/BTS for technical Ausbildungen is often preferred.
